source_text: Who are you, great mountain, before Zerubbabel, to set things straight? I will bring out the stone of inheritance—an equality of grace, its grace.”
reason: Isaiah explicitly brings mountains and hills low, whereas the supplied Zechariah addresses the great mountain before Zerubbabel and speaks of the stone of inheritance and grace. The particular leveling claim was not imported into Zechariah.

target_units.text: Every valley will be filled, and every mountain and hill will be brought low; all the crooked places will become straight, and the rough country will become plains.

source_text: Thus says the Lord Almighty: If it is impossible before this people’s remnant in those days, surely it will not also be impossible before Me? says the Lord Almighty.
reason: The supplied Jeremiah prayer says nothing can be hidden from God, rather than nothing being impossible. It was not retained as the proposed explicit impossibility parallel; Genesis 18:14 supplies an actually stated comparison instead.

target_units.text: O Lord, Thou madest heaven and earth by Thy great strength and Thy high, uplifted arm. Nothing can be hidden from Thee.

source_text: You will settle in a stronghold, prisoners of the gathering; in exchange for one day of your sojourn I will repay you double.
reason: Isaiah's supplied wording concerns inheriting land a second time and enduring joy. It does not explicitly state Zechariah's double repayment for one day of sojourn, so this proposed particular recompense link was not retained.

target_units.text: Thus they will inherit the land a second time, and everlasting joy will be over their head.

source_text: The Lord will save Judah’s dwellings as from the beginning, so that the boasting of David’s house and Jerusalem’s residents’ exaltation will not magnify itself over Judah.
reason: Paul's account of God choosing weak and despised things prevents flesh from boasting before Him. It does not establish Zechariah's particular concern that David's house and Jerusalem not exalt themselves over Judah; the broad anti-boasting principle was not retained as a sufficiently particular match.

target_units.text: But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong;
and God chose the lowborn things of the world and the despised things, the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are,
so that no flesh may boast before God.

source_text: I will pour upon David’s house and Jerusalem’s residents a spirit of grace and compassion. They will look toward Me because they danced in mockery, and mourn over him as over a beloved one; they will suffer grief as over a firstborn.
reason: John's cited Scripture concerns looking on the One whom they pierced. The supplied Zechariah instead says they will look toward Me because they danced in mockery. A claim that the native verse itself states piercing was not retained; no source-wording identity was assumed from the familiar quotation association.

target_units.text: And again another Scripture says, “They will look on the One whom they pierced.”

source_text: On that day every place will be opened in David’s house.
reason: Ezekiel expressly promises cleansing water, uncleanness removed and cleansing from idols. The supplied Zechariah unit says every place will be opened in David's house and does not mention a fountain or water. The proposed water correspondence is therefore unretained.

target_units.text: I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you will be cleansed from all your uncleannesses and all your idols. I will cleanse you.

source_text: On that day the prophets will be ashamed, each because of his vision when he prophesies; they will wear a hairy skin because they lied.
reason: Kings describes Elijah as a hairy man with a leather belt. Zechariah says lying prophets wear a hairy skin. The target does not explicitly describe the proposed matching garment, and the figures' clothing or identities were not equated.

target_units.text: They said to him, ‘A hairy man, with a leather belt fastened around his waist.’ He said, ‘This is Elijah the Tishbite.’

source_text: I will say to him, ‘What are these wounds between your hands?’ He will say, ‘The ones with which I was struck in my beloved house.’
reason: John describes Jesus' nail-marked hands and pierced side, whereas Zechariah's dialogue concerns wounds between the hands attributed to the beloved house after the discussion of false prophets. Neither the person nor the origin of the wounds was securely matched; the proposal remains unretained.

target_units.text: So the other disciples were saying to him, “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them, “Unless I see in His hands the mark of the nails and put my finger into the mark of the nails and put my hand into His side, I certainly will not believe.”
And after eight days His disciples were inside again, and Thomas with them. Jesus comes, the doors being shut, and stood in the midst and said, “Peace to you.”
Then He says to Thomas, “Bring your finger here and see My hands, and bring your hand and put it into My side; and do not become unbelieving, but believing.”

source_text: On that day His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives opposite Jerusalem to the east. The Mount of Olives will split, half of it toward the east and half toward the sea—a very great chasm; half the mountain will incline north and half south.
reason: Ezekiel places the Lord's glory on a mountain opposite the city but does not name it in this unit. Zechariah explicitly names the Mount of Olives and describes its division. An exact mountain identity or splitting parallel was not counted from the unnamed setting.

target_units.text: The Lord’s glory rose from the midst of the city and stood upon the mountain opposite the city.
